Timeline::add_duration¶

Back to Timeline API Reference

Signature¶

Timeline Timeline::add_duration(const Duration& duration) const

What It Does¶

Shifts every defined timestamp forward by the supplied duration.

This is the primary “move these timestamps later” surface on Timeline.

It works on:

  • a scalar moment

  • a 1D temporal vector

  • a higher-rank timeline, when the duration operand is broadcast-compatible

The result keeps the temporal shape of the timeline and only changes the instants.

Parameters¶

d

The duration to add.

Common construction patterns include:

  • pluss::duration::seconds(...)

  • pluss::duration::minutes(...)

  • pluss::duration::hours(...)

  • pluss::duration::days(...)

In practical use, the main toggle is not a boolean argument but the duration you construct:

  • minutes for intraday shifts

  • hours for session or timezone-style offsets

  • days for an exact multiple of 24 elapsed hours

Returns¶

Timeline A shifted timeline with the same shape and timezone label as the input.

Examples¶

Example 1. Add 90 minutes to one scalar timestamp.

auto out = scalar.add_duration(pluss::duration::minutes(90));
std::cout << pluss::timeline::print(out) << "\n";

Output¶

Timeline(shape=[], tz=UTC)
2024-11-01 10:30:00

Example 2. Add one hour to every timestamp in a 1D timeline.

auto out = base.add_duration(pluss::duration::hours(1));
std::cout << pluss::timeline::print(out) << "\n";

Output¶

Timeline(shape=[4], tz=UTC)
[ 2024-11-01 10:00:00, 2024-11-01 11:15:30, 2025-01-01 00:59:59, 2025-01-01 01:00:00 ]

Full Scope: Every Unit Factory, Same Instant¶

Every pluss::duration::* unit factory works here — they all just scale a fixed nanosecond offset, so the choice of factory is purely about how you want to express the shift, not a different code path. Starting from 1999-04-17T21:15:23Z:

const auto t0 = pluss::timeline::make("1999-04-17T21:15:23Z");
std::cout << pluss::timeline::print(t0 + pluss::duration::nanos(1)) << "\n";
std::cout << pluss::timeline::print(t0 + pluss::duration::microseconds(1)) << "\n";
std::cout << pluss::timeline::print(t0 + pluss::duration::milliseconds(1)) << "\n";
std::cout << pluss::timeline::print(t0 + pluss::duration::seconds(1)) << "\n";
std::cout << pluss::timeline::print(t0 + pluss::duration::minutes(1)) << "\n";
std::cout << pluss::timeline::print(t0 + pluss::duration::hours(1)) << "\n";
std::cout << pluss::timeline::print(t0 + pluss::duration::days(1)) << "\n";
std::cout << pluss::timeline::print(t0 + pluss::duration::weeks(1)) << "\n";

Output¶

plus_1ns  1999-04-17 21:15:23
plus_1us  1999-04-17 21:15:23
plus_1ms  1999-04-17 21:15:23
plus_1s   1999-04-17 21:15:24
plus_1min 1999-04-17 21:16:23
plus_1h   1999-04-17 22:15:23
plus_1d   1999-04-18 21:15:23
plus_1w   1999-04-24 21:15:23

pluss::timeline::print renders down to whole seconds, so the 1ns/1us/1ms shifts are real (the nanosecond count in total_nanoseconds() genuinely changes) but do not show up in this text rendering — inspect total_nanoseconds()/total_microseconds() directly if you need to see sub-second precision.

The motivating case — adding 3 hours to 21:15:23 — rolls the instant into the next calendar day:

std::cout << pluss::timeline::print(t0 + pluss::duration::hours(3)) << "\n";

Output¶

Timeline(shape=[], tz=UTC)
1999-04-18 00:15:23

This is plain fixed-offset nanosecond arithmetic on the UTC epoch axis; it has no concept of calendar irregularities. If you instead want “3 calendar days in a given timezone, respecting offset transitions,” or “add 1 calendar month,” use Timeline::add_days, Timeline::add_months, or Timeline::add_years. Those methods operate on local calendar fields rather than adding a fixed Duration.

Operator Sugar Is the Named Method, Not a Separate Path¶

t + d and t.add_duration(d) compute identically — verified by comparing them elementwise:

const auto via_operator = t0 + pluss::duration::hours(3);
const auto via_method = t0.add_duration(pluss::duration::hours(3));
std::cout << pluss::series::print(via_operator.eq(via_method)) << "\n";

Output¶

Series(shape=[], strides=[], dtype=bool, platform=cpu, numel=1, contiguous=true)
data=true

Addition is commutative at the public surface: both timeline + duration and duration + timeline return the same Timeline. The reverse form is useful when a duration expression naturally comes first; it is not a different kernel or a different broadcasting rule.

t += d and t -= d also exist, as compound-assignment sugar around the same two binary operators (*this = *this + d; return *this;), and are verified identical to them:

auto t_mut = t0;
t_mut += pluss::duration::hours(3);
std::cout << pluss::timeline::print(t_mut) << "\n";
std::cout << pluss::series::print(t_mut.eq(t0 + pluss::duration::hours(3))) << "\n";

Output¶

Timeline(shape=[], tz=UTC)
1999-04-18 00:15:23

Series(shape=[], strides=[], dtype=bool, platform=cpu, numel=1, contiguous=true)
data=true

Broadcasting¶

add_duration/operator+ use standard trailing-axis broadcasting. A scalar operand therefore pairs with every element of an N-D operand on the other side.

Example: a scalar Timeline plus a 1D Duration broadcasts to a 1D result.

const auto steps = pluss::duration::hours({1, 2, 3, 4});
std::cout << pluss::timeline::print(t0 + steps) << "\n";

Output¶

Timeline(shape=[4], tz=UTC)
[ 1999-04-17 22:15:23, 1999-04-17 23:15:23, 1999-04-18 00:15:23, 1999-04-18 01:15:23 ]

The reverse shape combination also broadcasts: a 1D Timeline plus a scalar Duration.

const auto t_vec = pluss::timeline::make({
    "2024-11-01T09:00:00Z", "2024-11-01T10:00:00Z",
    "2024-11-01T11:00:00Z", "2024-11-01T12:00:00Z",
});
std::cout << pluss::timeline::print(t_vec + pluss::duration::minutes(30)) << "\n";

Output¶

Timeline(shape=[4], tz=UTC)
[ 2024-11-01 09:30:00, 2024-11-01 10:30:00, 2024-11-01 11:30:00, 2024-11-01 12:30:00 ]

And matching shapes combine elementwise, not by broadcast:

std::cout << pluss::timeline::print(t_vec + steps) << "\n";

Output¶

Timeline(shape=[4], tz=UTC)
[ 2024-11-01 10:00:00, 2024-11-01 12:00:00, 2024-11-01 14:00:00, 2024-11-01 16:00:00 ]

Absent Instants¶

NaT propagates from either side of the addition: an absent instant or an absent (Duration::kNaT) duration both produce NaT:

const auto t_absent = pluss::timeline::make(""); // documented absent-instant text
std::cout << pluss::timeline::print(t_absent + pluss::duration::hours(1)) << "\n";

const auto d_absent = pluss::duration::nanos(pluss::Duration::kNaT);
std::cout << pluss::timeline::print(t0 + d_absent) << "\n";

Output¶

Timeline(shape=[], tz=UTC)
NaT

Timeline(shape=[], tz=UTC)
NaT

Timezone Handling¶

add_duration/operator+ always keep the tz label of the left-hand Timeline operand (Duration itself carries no timezone). The arithmetic still happens on the underlying UTC instant, so the printed wall-clock time reflects that timezone’s offset at each instant (including DST, when it applies):

const auto t0_ny = t0.tz_convert("America/New_York");
std::cout << pluss::timeline::print(t0_ny) << "\n";
std::cout << pluss::timeline::print(t0_ny + pluss::duration::hours(3)) << "\n";

Output¶

Timeline(shape=[], tz=America/New_York)
1999-04-17 17:15:23

Timeline(shape=[], tz=America/New_York)
1999-04-17 20:15:23

21:15:23 UTC is 17:15:23 in America/New_York under April 1999 DST (UTC-4); adding a fixed 3 hours lands on 20:15:23 in that same zone — the shift is still exactly 3 hours of elapsed time, the wall-clock display just reflects the timezone label.

Notes¶

  • Absent instants remain absent.

  • The timeline shape is preserved (subject to broadcasting, see above).

  • Crossing a date boundary is handled naturally by the underlying timestamp arithmetic, as shown by the verified 2024-12-31 to 2025-01-01 rollover in Example 2 above and the 21:15:23 to next-day 00:15:23 rollover above.

  • A shift outside the representable nanosecond epoch range throws; it never wraps into another date or into NaT.

  • Operator sugar also exists: t + d, and it is identical to add_duration, not an approximation of it. t += d is the compound-assignment form of the same thing.
